questions.stem: The official ideology of Tsarist rule from the 1830s, restated under Alexander III and Nicholas II, was summed up in the formula:
options: Liberty, Equality and Fraternity for all
Peace, Land and Bread
Church, Army and the Duma
Orthodoxy, Autocracy, Nationality
questions.explanation: Count Uvarov set out 'Orthodoxy, Autocracy, Nationality' in 1833 as the basis of Russian education and loyalty. It tied the Tsar's absolute power to the Orthodox Church and to Russian national identity. 'Peace, Land and Bread' was a Bolshevik slogan of 1917.

questions.stem: Konstantin Pobedonostsev, tutor to Nicholas II and lay head of the Holy Synod, influenced the young Tsar mainly by teaching that:
options: Russia should adopt a British-style constitution once industry had developed
the Orthodox Church should be separated from the state and the monarchy
the peasants should be given full ownership of the land they farmed
parliaments, a free press and elections were dangerous to Russia's stability
questions.explanation: Pobedonostsev was a leading conservative who argued that representative institutions and Western liberal ideas would destroy Russia. His influence helps explain Nicholas's reluctance to share power, even after 1905.

questions.stem: In January 1895 Nicholas II told representatives of the zemstvos that hopes of their taking part in government were 'senseless dreams'. This statement best shows:
options: his determination to preserve autocracy as he had inherited it
his plan to replace the zemstvos with an elected national parliament
his willingness to consult liberals once his reign was established
his belief that local government should pass to the Orthodox Church
questions.explanation: Early in his reign Nicholas made clear he would uphold autocracy as firmly as his father, disappointing liberals in the zemstvos (elected local councils). This set the pattern of refusing reform until forced.

questions.stem: The Okhrana in Tsarist Russia was:
options: the council of ministers that advised the Tsar on government policy
the elected local council that ran schools and roads in rural areas
the Cossack cavalry regiments used to guard the imperial family
the secret police, which watched and infiltrated opposition groups
questions.explanation: The Okhrana used informers and agents inside revolutionary parties, censorship of mail and arrests. Its methods could weaken opposition groups but also deepened hostility to the regime.

questions.stem: The 1897 census found that Great Russians made up only about 44 per cent of the Empire's population. Why was this significant for the regime?
options: Russification policies were imposed on a non-Russian majority, fuelling national opposition
The Tsar was forced to grant self-government to every national minority within the Empire
Non-Russians were excluded from conscription, which weakened the army before 1904
Russian peasants demanded that land be taken from the minorities and handed over to them
questions.explanation: Poles, Ukrainians, Finns, Jews, Georgians and many others resented policies imposing the Russian language and Orthodoxy. National grievances fed revolutionary and nationalist movements, such as the Jewish Bund and Polish socialists, and erupted in 1905.

questions.stem: By 1900, which feature of village life most limited peasant farming in central Russia?
options: Most peasants had moved into the towns, leaving the villages short of agricultural labour
The commune (mir) controlled and redistributed strips of land and shared tax liability
Peasants owned large private farms but could not sell their grain on foreign markets
Landlords had regained legal ownership of the serfs after the reforms were reversed
questions.explanation: The mir periodically redistributed land in scattered strips and was collectively responsible for taxes and redemption payments. This discouraged improvement, while rapid population growth increased land hunger.

questions.stem: Why did conditions in Russia's fast-growing industrial cities create a revolutionary threat by 1905?
options: Workers had won the vote in city councils and used it to defy the Tsar
Workers faced long hours and crowded housing, and strikes and trade unions were illegal
Factory owners had formed their own party in the Duma to demand a republic
Industrial workers already made up the large majority of the Empire's population by 1900
questions.explanation: Workers were concentrated in large factories in St Petersburg and Moscow, with poor pay and housing and no legal way to bargain. That concentration made them open to socialist organisation, although they remained a small minority of the population.

questions.stem: Around 1901-1903 the police official Sergei Zubatov sponsored workers' organisations that pursued economic gains under police supervision. What does this policy, and Gapon's later police-approved assembly, best suggest?
options: The regime was preparing to legalise independent trade unions and the right to strike
The regime had decided that socialist parties should be allowed to take part in elections
The regime believed that industrial workers were far too few to pose any threat to autocracy
The regime tried to steer workers away from politics, but the bodies could turn against it
questions.explanation: 'Police socialism' aimed to keep workers loyal by meeting economic grievances while banning political action. It backfired: strikes grew, and Gapon's assembly led the march that ended in Bloody Sunday in January 1905.

questions.stem: How did the Russo-Japanese War of 1904-1905 contribute to the crisis of 1905?
options: Expected to be a quick victory, it brought a string of defeats that discredited the regime
It forced the Tsar to abdicate in favour of his brother soon after the fall of Port Arthur
It ended with Japan occupying Vladivostok and imposing a constitution on the Tsar
It led the army to mutiny as a whole and join the workers of St Petersburg
questions.explanation: Russia's leaders underestimated Japan. The fall of Port Arthur, defeat at Mukden and the destruction of the fleet at Tsushima humiliated the government and added to economic hardship, feeding the unrest of 1905.

questions.stem: Tsar Alexander II was assassinated in 1881 by members of which revolutionary group?
options: the Kadets
the Octobrists
People's Will
the Bolsheviks
questions.explanation: People's Will (Narodnaya Volya) was a populist group that used terrorism. The Bolsheviks emerged in 1903 and the Kadets and Octobrists were liberal parties formed in 1905.

questions.stem: Which consequence of the assassination of Alexander II most shaped the reign of Nicholas II?
options: The Orthodox Church lost its influence after failing to protect the Tsar's life
Alexander III's counter-reforms and repression set the model of rule Nicholas inherited
The new Tsar granted a constitution to win back the loyalty of educated society
The populists took over local government and began redistributing land to peasants
questions.explanation: Alexander III blamed his father's reforms for encouraging revolution and ruled through repression, censorship and Russification. Nicholas, raised in this atmosphere and taught by Pobedonostsev, saw autocracy as a sacred duty.

questions.stem: During late 1904 liberals, many active in the zemstvos and linked to the Union of Liberation, held a series of public banquets. Their main demand was:
options: workers' control of factories through soviets
a constitution and an elected national assembly
the immediate overthrow of the Tsar by armed revolt
the transfer of all land to peasant communes
questions.explanation: The banquet campaign, timed to the 40th anniversary of the 1864 judicial reforms, used legal gatherings to call for civil rights and an elected parliament. Liberals wanted constitutional monarchy, not revolution or socialism.

questions.stem: In July 1904 the Interior Minister, Vyacheslav von Plehve, was killed by a bomb. Which party's terrorist wing carried out the assassination?
options: the Socialist Revolutionaries
the Social Democrats (Mensheviks)
the Constitutional Democrats
the Union of the Russian People
questions.explanation: The Socialist Revolutionaries' Combat Organisation used assassination against officials. The Marxist Social Democrats generally rejected individual terror, the Kadets were liberals, and the Union of the Russian People was a right-wing monarchist group.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly distinguishes the Octobrists from the Kadets after 1905?
options: Octobrists boycotted the Duma entirely; Kadets refused to stand candidates in elections
Octobrists accepted the October Manifesto as enough; Kadets wanted a true parliamentary system
Octobrists wanted a socialist republic; Kadets wanted to restore unlimited autocracy
Octobrists represented industrial workers; Kadets represented the landless peasantry
questions.explanation: The Octobrists, led by Alexander Guchkov, were moderate conservatives satisfied with the Manifesto. The Kadets (Constitutional Democrats), led by Pavel Milyukov, wanted ministers responsible to the Duma and wider reform.

questions.stem: Troops fired on striking miners at the Lena goldfields in Siberia in April 1912. What was the main consequence?
options: The legalisation of trade unions to prevent any repeat of the shootings
The resignation of Nicholas II's chief minister, Pyotr Stolypin, in protest
A new wave of strikes that grew larger each year until the outbreak of war
The immediate dissolution of the Fourth Duma and the arrest of its deputies
questions.explanation: The shootings provoked protest strikes across the Empire, and labour unrest rose sharply in 1912-1914. Stolypin had already been assassinated in 1911.

questions.stem: The St Petersburg Soviet of Workers' Deputies, formed in October 1905, was:
options: a council of delegates elected in factories to coordinate the general strike
a committee of Duma deputies appointed by the Tsar to draft a constitution
a group of senior army officers who planned to replace the Tsar with his brother
a union of zemstvo liberals that organised the banquet campaign of 1904
questions.explanation: The Soviet coordinated strikes and published its own newspaper. Trotsky became its leading figure. Its members were arrested in December 1905, but the model of soviets returned in 1917.

questions.stem: Nicholas II issued the October Manifesto in 1905 mainly because:
options: his generals refused to serve on unless the peasants were given the land
a general strike had paralysed the country and Witte advised concession
the Duma had voted to depose him unless he granted civil liberties
the war with Japan was going well and he could afford to be generous
questions.explanation: The October general strike stopped railways, factories and services. Witte argued that the alternative to concessions was a military dictatorship that might fail. The Duma did not yet exist, and the war had ended in defeat.

questions.stem: Which factor best explains why the regime could crush the remaining revolutionaries in December 1905 and early 1906?
options: The army stayed loyal, and peace with Japan allowed troops to be used at home
The workers' parties agreed to stop all strikes once the First Duma was elected
Peasants supported the government because they had been given ownership of the land
Foreign powers sent troops to St Petersburg to restore the Tsar's authority
questions.explanation: Once the war ended, loyal regiments crushed the Moscow rising in December 1905 and punitive expeditions restored order in the countryside. A large French loan in 1906 also helped. Peasant unrest continued into 1906.

questions.stem: In December 1905 an armed workers' rising in Moscow was put down by Guards troops, including the Semyonovsky Regiment. What did this show?
options: The Tsar had lost control of Moscow permanently to the revolutionary parties
The army refused to fire on workers once the October Manifesto was issued
With the army's support, the regime could still defeat revolution by force
The workers could defeat the army if they were armed and led by the Soviet
questions.explanation: The Presnya district was shelled and the rising collapsed. The lesson of 1905 was that the regime survived while the army stayed loyal; in February 1917 the garrison's mutiny was decisive.

questions.stem: At the Battle of Tannenberg in August 1914:
options: German forces surrounded and destroyed Russia's Second Army in East Prussia
Russian forces captured Berlin's eastern defences and forced a German retreat
the Austro-Hungarian army was destroyed by a Russian offensive in Galicia
Russia's Baltic fleet was sunk by German submarines near the Finnish coast
questions.explanation: Samsonov's Second Army was encircled and largely destroyed, and Samsonov took his own life. The defeat, early in the war, showed the Russian army's weaknesses in command, communications and supply.

questions.stem: During the 'Great Retreat' of 1915 the Russian army:
options: retreated from Petrograd, which was occupied by German forces until 1917
abandoned its alliance with Britain and France and sought a separate peace
lost Russian Poland and other western territories amid severe shortages of shells
withdrew from Galicia after a mutiny over Nicholas taking personal command
questions.explanation: German and Austro-Hungarian offensives drove Russia out of Poland, with Warsaw falling in August 1915. Millions of refugees moved east, and the defeats led Nicholas to take command of the army himself.

questions.stem: In August 1915 a majority of Duma deputies formed the Progressive Bloc. Its central demand was:
options: an immediate peace with Germany and Austria-Hungary without annexations
the transfer of all land to the peasants and of factories to the workers
a government of ministers who had the confidence of the nation and the Duma
the immediate abdication of Nicholas II in favour of his young son, Alexei
questions.explanation: The Bloc, led by Milyukov, united moderates and liberals behind a 'ministry of confidence' to run the war better. Nicholas refused and suspended the Duma in September 1915, alienating the patriotic moderates who might have supported him.

questions.stem: Zemgor, the joint committee of the zemstvo and town unions led by Prince Lvov, helped weaken the regime during the war because it:
options: refused to cooperate with the army until the Tsar agreed to share power with the Duma
secretly negotiated with Germany for a separate peace behind the government's back
supplied the army and wounded effectively, showing the public could organise better than the state
organised strikes in munitions factories to force the government to end the war quickly
questions.explanation: Zemgor ran hospitals and organised supplies, gaining public respect while the government was blamed for shortages. Its leaders, including Lvov, became the Provisional Government in 1917.

questions.stem: How did the government's methods of paying for the war contribute to unrest by 1916?
options: Selling the crown jewels abroad angered patriotic Russians living in the cities
Printing money and borrowing pushed prices far ahead of most workers' wages
Heavy new income taxes on peasants led them to stop growing grain for sale
Seizing factory profits caused owners to close plants and dismiss workers
questions.explanation: The state lost revenue (including from its ban on vodka sales in 1914) and covered spending with paper money and loans. Inflation outpaced wages, and urban workers suffered while shortages grew.

questions.stem: The Brusilov Offensive of 1916 against Austria-Hungary is significant because it was:
options: the offensive that knocked Austria-Hungary right out of the war in the summer of 1916
the first battle in which Russian troops refused orders and joined the soldiers' soviets
Russia's most successful offensive of the war, yet its huge losses deepened war-weariness
a total failure that ended with Austria-Hungary occupying Kiev and most of Ukraine that year
questions.explanation: Brusilov's attack in Galicia gained ground and badly damaged the Austro-Hungarian army, but Russia suffered enormous casualties and could not exploit its success. Austria-Hungary stayed in the war, propped up by Germany.

questions.stem: In December 1916 Grigori Rasputin was murdered by:
options: Bolshevik agents acting on Lenin's orders from Switzerland
German spies who feared his influence over the Tsar
soldiers of the Petrograd garrison during a mutiny
a group of aristocrats including Prince Felix Yusupov
questions.explanation: Yusupov, the right-wing deputy Purishkevich and Grand Duke Dmitri killed Rasputin, hoping to save the monarchy from his scandalous influence. The murder showed that even members of the elite had turned against the court.

questions.stem: On 1-2 March 1917, the chief of staff, General Alekseev, consulted the front commanders by telegram. What did they advise Nicholas to do?
options: Make an immediate peace with Germany and return to the capital
Hand power to the Petrograd Soviet until elections could be held
Abdicate, to keep the army together and continue the war
March on Petrograd with loyal troops and dissolve the Duma
questions.explanation: The generals believed abdication was the only way to restore order and keep fighting. Losing the support of his own high command was decisive in Nicholas's decision.

questions.stem: When Nicholas II signed his abdication at Pskov on 2 March 1917, he gave up the throne:
options: to the Petrograd Soviet, which he asked to call a Constituent Assembly
for himself and his son, naming his brother Grand Duke Michael as successor
for himself only, so that his son Alexei became Tsar under a regency
to the Duma, which he asked to choose a new dynasty to rule Russia
questions.explanation: Nicholas first intended to abdicate in favour of Alexei, but, concerned about his son's haemophilia and separation from the family, changed the act the same day to name Michael. This added to the confusion about the succession.

questions.stem: Why did Grand Duke Michael's response on 3 March 1917 mark the end of the Romanov dynasty?
options: He handed the crown to Alexei, who was too young to rule
He declined the throne unless a future Constituent Assembly offered it to him
He accepted the throne but was arrested by the Petrograd Soviet within hours
He fled abroad without replying, so the Duma at once declared Russia a republic
questions.explanation: Duma leaders warned Michael they could not guarantee his safety. He refused to accept power unless an elected Constituent Assembly chose a monarchy, leaving authority with the Provisional Government.

questions.stem: The first head of the Provisional Government, formed from the Duma's Provisional Committee in March 1917, was:
options: Prince Georgy Lvov
Alexander Kerensky
Pavel Milyukov
Mikhail Rodzianko
questions.explanation: Lvov, head of Zemgor, became prime minister. Milyukov was foreign minister and Kerensky minister of justice; Kerensky became prime minister in July 1917. Rodzianko was President of the Duma.

questions.stem: Which weakness of the Provisional Government was present from the moment power was transferred to it in March 1917?
options: It had been appointed by Nicholas II, so revolutionaries saw it as a Tsarist body
It was dominated by Bolsheviks, which alarmed the army and the Allied powers
It had already signed a peace with Germany, which outraged patriotic Russians
It was not elected and saw itself as temporary until a Constituent Assembly met
questions.explanation: The Provisional Government drew its authority from Duma politicians, not elections, and postponed big decisions such as land reform until a Constituent Assembly. It also had to share power with the Petrograd Soviet.

questions.stem: In the 'optimist' and 'pessimist' debate about late Tsarist Russia, which argument belongs to the pessimist side?
options: The renewed strike wave of 1912-1914 shows society was polarising before the war began
Rapid industrial growth and Stolypin's reforms show Russia was modernising successfully
The Duma was gradually turning the autocracy into a constitutional monarchy by 1914
Without the strains of the First World War the monarchy would probably have survived
questions.explanation: Pessimists such as Leopold Haimson argued that by 1914 Russia was deeply divided between workers and educated society and between society and the state, so revolution was likely anyway. Optimists stress pre-war growth and reform and see the war as decisive.

questions.stem: A historian argues that the fall of the Romanovs owed more to Nicholas II's personal failings than to Russia's structural problems. Which evidence best supports this view?
options: His refusal of a ministry of confidence in 1915 drove loyal moderates into opposition
Industrial workers were concentrated in a few large cities with poor living conditions
Russia's railways could not carry enough food and fuel to the cities during the war
The peasants' land hunger had been growing since the emancipation of the serfs
questions.explanation: Rejecting the Progressive Bloc was a personal choice that cost Nicholas the support of patriotic liberals. The other options are long-term structural problems that would have challenged any ruler.

questions.stem: In 2000 the Russian Orthodox Church canonised Nicholas II and his family as 'passion-bearers'. For a historian, this is best seen as an example of:
options: the official Soviet interpretation of the fall of the dynasty
a court verdict on the causes of the February Revolution
a changing representation of the Romanovs in post-Soviet Russia
new archival evidence proving that Nicholas was an effective ruler
questions.explanation: Canonisation honoured the family for the manner of their deaths in 1918, not for Nicholas's rule. In Soviet times the Tsar was presented as a tyrant; after 1991 more sympathetic representations emerged, and the remains of most of the family were reburied in St Petersburg in 1998.
